en-01-tip.caption:
Here is a question that decides how well you sleep: what did the business actually make last month? Most owners cannot answer it without going to look, and the going to look is the bit that never happens.

It is rarely about the size of the business. A one-van operation with current books is calmer than a six-figure one guessing. Three answers do most of the work: what you earned, what is still owed to you, and what is going out before the end of the month. Those three, in front of you, early.

That is most of what we actually do. Not clever schemes. Numbers you can trust, soon enough to change something while it still matters, and someone to talk them through with when they say something you did not expect.
en-01-tip.ask: Send this to an owner who could use a quieter week.
en-01-tip.title: The quiet week is the one where you know the numbers

en-02-acq.caption:
Most people have had the year-end email. An attachment, a lot of columns, a polite line asking you to sign. Nobody reads it, because nobody wrote it to be read.

We do the other thing. We go through your figures with you, out loud, in plain English. Which month was the odd one and why. Where the money actually went, as opposed to where you thought it went. What your margin does when you take the one big client out of the picture. Questions you are allowed to interrupt with, because that is the point of the conversation.

It changes what the numbers are for. A set of accounts filed is a duty. A set of accounts explained is a decision you can make: put the price up, drop the job that looks busy and pays badly, hire in March rather than June. Same figures either way. The difference is whether anybody ever told you what they said.

And the filing dates still get met while we are at it.

The first conversation is free and lasts 30 minutes.
en-02-acq.ask: Save this for the next time a set of accounts lands and means nothing to you.
en-02-acq.title: Your figures, explained out loud, in plain English

en-03-acq.caption:
A lot of company directors are quietly being looked after twice, or not at all. One firm does the company. Somebody else, or nobody, does their own return. Each side assumes the other has the whole picture, and the dividend that was voted in March is the thing that falls down the gap.

With us it is one desk. The person who prepares the company accounts is the person who prepares your Self Assessment. They already know what salary came out, what dividends were voted and when, what you put in and took back. Nothing has to be explained twice, and nothing has to be reconciled by email between two firms who have never met.

It is quieter at the year end, and it is cheaper in the way that matters: no second firm charging you to learn what the first one already knows.

We watch both sets of dates so you are not holding them in your head.

The first conversation is free and lasts 30 minutes.
en-03-acq.ask: Save this if your company and your own return currently sit with two different people.
en-03-acq.title: One desk for the company and for your own return

en-04-acq.caption:
Most owners are not bad at bookkeeping. They are doing bookkeeping that was designed, by nobody in particular, to need them every evening.

So we change the design. Receipts are photographed the moment they are handed over, by whoever is holding them, and the paper can go in the bin on the way out of the shop. The bank comes in by itself rather than being typed. The things that repeat every month are set up once and then simply happen. What is left for you is minutes a week, on your phone, standing up.

The real gain is not tidiness. It is that the records are current, so the figures mean something when you look at them, and nothing has to be reconstructed months later from memory and a folded pile of paper.

We set it up with you, we check it is still working, and we keep an eye on the filing dates while it runs.

The first conversation is free and lasts 30 minutes.
en-04-acq.ask: Share this with the one who still does the paperwork at ten at night.
en-04-acq.title: Set it up once and you stop keeping paper at all

en-05-edu.caption:
55p a mile for the first 10,000 business miles you drive, and 25p a mile after that. Motorcycles are 24p. That 55p is the new rate, up from 45p, and it applies from 6 April 2026.

Here is the trap this winter. The return you are filing by 31 January 2027 covers 2025-26, and for that year the first-band rate is still 45p. Use 55p on it and every mileage claim on the return is wrong. 55p belongs to the year you are living in now, not the year you are reporting on.

Flat rates mean you claim pence per mile instead of adding up fuel, insurance, servicing and repairs. You keep a mileage log, and that is the record. Tolls, the congestion charge and parking sit outside the rate and are claimed separately.

Working from home has flat rates too: 10 pounds a month for 25 to 50 hours, 18 pounds for 51 to 100, 26 pounds for 101 hours or more. Below 25 hours a month you cannot use it at all, and it never covers your phone or your internet.

Excluded: limited companies, and partnerships with a company as a partner. You also cannot use the mileage rate on a vehicle you have ever claimed capital allowances on, and once you use flat rates for a vehicle you stay on them until you replace it.
en-05-edu.ask: Save this one, because the two mileage rates are easy to swap by mistake.
en-05-edu.title: 55p a mile now, 45p on the return you file in January

en-06-edu.caption:
If you are a director of a UK company, Companies House now has to know that you are a real, identified person. You prove it once, and what comes back is an 11-character personal code. It belongs to you rather than to a company, and the same code covers every directorship you hold.

What it costs depends entirely on the route. Doing it yourself with Companies House through GOV.UK One Login is free of charge - online, or in person at a participating Post Office with the right documents. There is also a paid route: an authorised provider can verify you instead, and may charge a fee for it. So 'it is free' is true of one route and not the other.

Nobody can do the identity check on your behalf. Companies House says it cannot verify people itself, and an accountant cannot verify you either - once you have your code, your accountant can file using it, but getting it is yours to do.

The code does not then file itself. A director gives it in the company's next confirmation statement. Someone who owns or controls the company gives it through the service for that, inside their own 14-day window. A director of four companies does it four times. If you are both, you do both, separately.

And the timing, because this is the part that has moved. The 12-month transition period for people already on the register started on 18 November 2025 and is over: it ended at the end of 17 November 2026, a week before you are reading this. Companies House says all companies must have met the requirement, or be on a compliance or enforcement pathway, by the end of March 2027. A director who carries on acting unverified is committing an offence, and the first prosecutions have already been through a magistrates' court.

Outside the requirement: shareholders who do not control the company, employees, company secretaries, and sole traders, who are not on the register at all.
en-06-edu.ask: Save this if you are a director and that code is still sitting unused.
en-06-edu.title: Directors: the year to prove who you are ended on 17 November

en-07-edu.caption:
Directors take money out of their own company all the time and call it a loan. The line to know is £10,000.

If everything you owe the company, added together, stays under £10,000 for the whole tax year, there is no taxable benefit and nothing to report. An overdrawn director's loan account counts towards it. So does a loan to a relative.

Cross the line and the exemption is gone completely. The benefit is then worked out on the whole loan, not only the part above £10,000, using HMRC's official rate of interest, which is 3.75% from 6 April 2026. And it is tested at any moment in the year, not on the balance sitting there at your year end, so a short spike in the middle of the summer is enough to do it.

One more thing, because it catches people. This is a separate matter from the corporation tax charge on a loan to a participator - somebody with a stake in the company - which has its own rate and its own nine-month repayment rule. One overdrawn account can bring both. The £10,000 has nothing to do with that one.

Outside the £10,000 rule: loans made in place of pay, under salary sacrifice, which have to be reported whatever the balance. Loans already exempt on other grounds do not need the rule at all.
en-07-edu.ask: Keep this one to hand before you take the next round out of the company.
en-07-edu.title: Under £10,000 all year and there is nothing to report

en-08-joke.caption:
He rang up delighted. The whole Christmas party is going through the business, he said, so bring who you like.

Then the guest list arrived. His cousin. His barber. A DJ he met once.

What can count is an annual function for your own staff, within limits, and open to all of them. Start adding the people you simply like and the shape of the thing changes, and so does the tax treatment. Plus ones and other guests are their own question, and worth asking before you book rather than after.

Have the party. Have a good one. Just tell us the guest list first, and we will tell you which part of it the business is actually buying.
en-08-joke.ask: Share this with whoever is organising the party.
en-08-joke.title: He is putting the whole Christmas party through the business

en-09-joke.caption:
He set up one address for enquiries, one for invoices, and one he made in a hurry at the bank. Very organised. Three front doors.

He has not opened any of them since the summer. So the things that come on paper instead end up on the windowsill, behind the kettle, going slowly yellow.

This is the most ordinary problem in small business and it is not laziness. Post arrives in four places, so none of them is the place, so nobody checks any of them. The fix is boring and it works: one address that everything points at, one person who opens it, one evening a week. Change it at the bank, at HMRC, at Companies House, on the van.

Nothing that arrives at a company is ever urgent in week one and expensive in week one. It becomes expensive by sitting there.
en-09-joke.ask: Share this with whoever has three inboxes and reads none of them.
en-09-joke.title: Three email addresses for the business, and nobody opens one

en-10-quote.caption:
Thoreau is writing about money, but not in the way people expect. He is saying a price is not really measured in pounds. It is measured in the hours of your life you hand over to earn them.

It is a useful test for a business owner, and an uncomfortable one. The cheap client who takes three times the work is not cheap. The job you took because the number looked good, which then ate your evenings for a month, cost more than it paid. The thing you are putting off because it is boring is quietly charging you interest.

We see this in the numbers more often than people would guess. Revenue up, life down. Those are not the same direction, and only one of them shows on the bank statement.
en-10-quote.ask: Save this one and read it again when you next quote a price.
en-10-quote.title: A price is paid in hours, not in pounds
